I approach the discussion of this motion on behalf of my party in an objective way. I am going to restrict myself to some matters to which reference was not made by the hon. gentleman. It would be an easy course to
[Mr. Dlefenbaker.l

follow for the members of the opposition to stand in this house and place the responsibility for this measure upon the government, hoping thereby to take advantage of some of the honest fears of former members of the armed forces and their dependents who are concerned over the eventualities which may occur. That is not the course which the Progressive Conservative party intends to follow. We desire to be objective. I desire to discuss this matter in a nonpartisan spirit, for after all this is a measure upon which the future and the freedom of our country depends. Partisanship has no place in frank discussion.
I hope that we shall not be mistaken in the course we shall take and that what has been done will be a triumph for faith rather than a victory for doubt; that we will prove that the soul of freedom is strong enough to meet the needs of the turbulent present; that out of the agreements that have been made, out of the ashes of frustration in the negotiations with the U.S.S.R. to which the minister made reference will rise a new world achieved by the extension of the area of collective security.
The Canadian people are interested in foreign affairs, as is evidenced by the fact that editorials in our papers and observations of those who write on the subject of international affairs are receiving more and more attention. I believe a greater dissemination of information on international affairs should be made to the Canadian people than is furnished by the magazine External Affairs. Useful as it is, in recent months it has betrayed evidence of self-congratulation of those associated with the Department of External Affairs.
We are now in a period of coexistence. Recently the minister gave a description of coexistence which I thought was particularly appropriate. He said that the U.S.S.R. idea of coexistence was that of Jonah and the whale. There is no denying the fact that the U.S.S.R. has adopted a new strategy of sweet words, a coaxing attitude and a smiling Molotov. This change of attitude has become the unsecret weapon of the U.S.S.R. The Soviets smile, but at the same time they try to create and foster discord among the members of the United Nations. Coexistence is a seductive word. One of their smartest pieces of propaganda ever developed is the use of that word.
We believe in coexistence. Coexistence means to us the handshake, but not the embrace. The U.S.S.R. has shown the smiling face lately while it continues its aggression by proxy. It has rejoined the international labour organization; it has joined UNESCO; it has offered a conducted welcome to those

who visit the U.S.S.R.; it has allowed the wives of diplomats to migrate; it has joined in the unanimous votes in the United Nations on disarmament, and in the setting up of an international atomic energy agency. It has been sweet and conciliatory; it has practised flattery and blandishment. It even offered to join NATO, which was analogous to Satan joining the anti-hell society. It is trying to coax by promises and to threaten by intimidation.
There have been tremendous changes since parliament last met. There has been the settlement in Trieste and the Saar; there have been the Anglo-Egyptian settlement and agreement and the Persian settlement. But the U.S.S.R. has not changed its objective. Nothing has been more serious than the revelation that for the last six months the secretary of the defence council in France each day delivered to the U.S.S.R. copies of the minutes of the meetings of the national defence council of France, and minutes which revealed the strategy of NATO.
The objectives of communism are unchanged. This is revealed by the declarations of the governments of the U.S.S.R. and the so-called republics of Poland, Czechoslovakia, the Ukraine, the German democratic republic, Hungary, Roumania, Bulgaria and Albania. It takes courage to be a member of parliament in any of those countries. In the 1950 election, of the members elected to the Volkskammer, in East Germany 49 have been shot and 59 have had to leave that country as refugees. I am just going to give one or two quotations from the declaration. It gives evidence of care in its preparation, power in its vision and deception in its concept. It states:
The Paris agreements are directly at variance with the possibilities for further relaxation of the international tension which has come to light of late.
Later:
Not only are these agreements alien to the interests of the German people, but they are directly spearheaded against the German working class, are designated to suppress democratic forces in western Germany.
These agreements create a military bloc of aggressive circles of U.S.A., Britain and France with German militarism.
It maintains that the agreements are the product of great monopolies.
Then it says further:
Rejection of plans for remilitarization of western Germany and her integration in military alignments, which would remove the main obstacle to the reunion of Germany on peace-loving and democratic principles;
And still further it says that the real security of Europe can be assured if instead of following this course we operate in co-operation with all European states irrespective of
North Atlantic Treaty
their social and state systems and thereby make possible by combined efforts of European states the safeguarding of peace in Europe.
My hon. friend has stated that meetings with the Soviets seldom lead to agreement. A simple example of ineffective negotiation is what has been done on the Austrian peace treaty. There were 352 meetings without settlement. Finally-and the threat is at the end-it says:
Our peoples are confident In their strength, in their inexhaustible resources. The forces of peace and socialism are stronger and more solidly united than ever before. Any attempts to attack, to unleash war and to disturb the peaceful life of our peoples, will receive crushing rebuff.
First there is the cajolement and then the threat. They fear rearmament in West Germany, with 175 divisions of their own under arms and 80 divisions in their satellite countries.
Is German rearmament a new idea? It was first brought to the attention of the world by Ernest Bevin, who used these words some four and a half years ago:
If West Germany is to be defended it seems to us only fair and reasonable that the people of Western Germany should help in their own defence.
On September 14, 1951, the three foreign ministers made the following declaration after the Washington conference:
The three foreign ministers declare that their government's aim is the inclusion of a democratic Germany on a basis of equality in a continental European community which itself will form part of a constantly developing Atlantic community.
Out of that declaration grew the European defence community. It provided for the mobilization of 500,000 men and other forces to which the minister made reference. It provided an executive cabinet of all the member nations, a court of justice, an economic and social council, a house of parliament with two chambers, a senate and a house of representatives. It assured effective control of any German army that might be mobilized, because such an army would be part of an international army. The armed forces from Germany would find themselves not allocated to their own units but placed indiscriminately among the forces of other nations in an international army in much the same way as foreigners who join the French foreign legion lose their national identity in a common loyalty. France defeated that plan, the great concept of 500 years. It was defeated by France whose statesmen first gave it outline. As the minister has said, a vacuum was created at that time, and then the NATO defence system was put in a position to take its place. Mr. Dulles has set forth the basic

North Atlantic Treaty
and stubborn facts with regard to what followed the defeat of EDC last September.
Effective military defence of Europe called for a substantial military contribution by Germany; Germany could not be subjected indefinitely to discriminations relating to her sovereignty and her right of self-defence; the prevention of war between neighbouring nations with a long record of fighting could be dependably achieved only by merging certain functions of their governments in supranational institutions.
Out of those views and out of the wise leadership of Sir Anthony Eden, to which tribute was paid by my hon. friend, and the leadership of Sir Winston Churchill, out of what appeared to be the degradation of defeat of collective security for generations, grew the inception of the present system which, imperfect as it is, represents in my opinion the best of any of the alternatives that are offered.
NATO has been a pronounced success when the situation in Europe four years ago is compared with today. When you visit the headquarters, and when you see that leader of the democracies, General Gruenther, you realize the difficulties that he must have had in bringing together the clashing elements of national jealousy and the formidable developments that have taken place. Indeed, when General Montgomery was in Canada a little over a year ago he said this:

Canadians recognize NATO as one of those things that was evolved out of a Canadian concept.
-is the strong right arm of UNO. Without NATO, UNO would achieve little. Together they can achieve much. Both are necessary. If NATO had come into being earlier there would have been no second war. In the strengthening of NATO lies the best hope of preventing a third world war.
I consider that the strengthening of NATO on the political side for purposes beyond those of defence is all-important.
The minister said the same today. I ask him now, to say when he replies, what has been done to make NATO an institution that can be held together only if we realize that we must merge some of our economic problems within the purview of its concept. What has been done and what is being done to make NATO an institution not altogether military in its concept? General Gruenther said this, and I think his statement is worthy to be quoted. He shows no aggressiveness in his attitude to the U.S.S.R. He shows firmness and statesmanlike vision. He said this while the London meeting was under way:
West German armament and the tactical use of the atom bomb would produce in three or four years a reasonably good chance of preventing the Soviet union from overrunning Europe. West German rearmament was necessary because the western powers needed a shield strong enough to hold

while reserves were being mobilized. Tactical atomic bombing was needed to compensate for the immense numerical superiority of the Soviet bloc.
There is the background. The discussion of these agreements and protocols falls, I believe, into the ambit of four or five subjects with which I am going to deal now in somewhat lesser detail than I had expected, in view of the explanations given by the minister. What is the essence of the terms of these agreements? What are the safeguards against the resurgence of German militarism? What are the dangers if the projected course contemplated by these agreements is followed? What are the alternatives to these agreements?
The minister reviewed the agreements, and I am not going to do so again except to make one or two references. He set forth what the agreements provided for and he set forth some of the safeguards. The western European union will set up an, agency for the control of armaments. The council will make an annual report on its activities setting out the statistics of the various countries and the land and air forces necessary to be provided after consultation with each of the countries. The supreme allied commander in Europe will have entire control over the armies that will be raised, their deployment, their use, and above all, as the minister said, the logistics, which is simply a term that implies and contemplates those things upon which armies march. Particularly, as I see it, the gas and the oil necessary for the instruments of war will be entirely under the control of the general commanding in Europe who can turn the tap either on or off as need requires.
The minister then mentioned the fact that Germany agrees not to manufacture atomic, biological or chemical weapons except with the unanimous agreement of the other members of the organization. For some reason the minister left out three very important words. The undertaking of Germany is not to manufacture these things within its own territory. I am going to ask the minister a question later as to why it was necessary to permit Germany to manufacture these things outside her own territory.
The agency that is to be set up to control rearmament will appoint a director who will gather and examine national statistics and budgetary information, and have before him also a full record of the types of armaments being produced. All forces, as I said a moment ago, will be under the supreme commander. The location of all forces will be determined after consultation with NATO. These, in short, are the safeguards, coupled with a declaration by Germany that she will

do nothing of an aggressive nature, and that she will live true to the principles of the United Nations Organization, in particular article 2 thereof. She undertakes also that she will never do anything to retrieve her lost territories or to reunify Germany. Of course these declarations, without safeguards, could well prove in the future to be hollow promises, unkept as were some other promises and undertakings of Germany in the past.
Britain made a great sacrifice in order to achieve this agreement. To keep the United States in Europe, to maintain the hopes and faith of France, Britain departed from her position of several hundred years and entered into an undertaking to remain in Europe for a period of some 40 years. Some of us were given to understand by the press of our country that this undertaking had also been given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on behalf of Canada. The minister has stated today that he did not go that far, but what he said in effect, as I understand it, is that Canada will make the necessary contribution in order to live within the concept of the agreement entered into.
For 500 years Britain has always been of Europe and yet not in Europe. Now she becomes both, in the interests of world peace. Will' the controls work? Will the annual review protect from resurgent militarism? All that we can do is to believe that the agreements will be carried out, policed as they will be by full inspection and reinforced by careful examination of the budget of West Germany. Lord Ismay, speaking in London last November, said that the annual review has been effective in so far as the nations now members of NATO are concerned. He went on to say:
It is extraordinary, when you come to think of it, that countries should be prepared not only to lay the details of their national military production and fiscal programs before their partners, but also to be cross-examined upon them. Never has the principle of alliance been carried to such a pitch.
If the U.S.S.R. would accept similar inspection, might we not hope to achieve what the minister stated was the first aim and purpose of the democratic nations of the world today, namely, the abolition as an instrument of war for all time of atomic and hydrogen bombs? What are the dangers? The minister has pointed them out-Scylla and Charybdis. Lord Ismay, when he affixed his name to the agreements, used his personal seal upon which was inscribed this motto:	"Have no fear". We have fears.
While every eventuality cannot be covered by an agreement, I believe with the minister that what the agreement does is to cover
North Atlantic Treaty
everything within the contemplation of the nations who fear a resurgence of militarism, everything within the limitations of the sovereignty of another nation.
I cannot believe, sir-and I am leaving my own country now when I say this-that Sir Winston Churchill, after all the years that he warned of the dangers of militarism in Germany, can now be appeased by an uncertain agreement. I cannot believe that Sir Anthony Eden, who gave two brothers in the first great war and his son in the last, is going to be deceived into entering into agreements that have in their being the germ of another war. This is what Eden said:
There are In these agreements all the safeguards it has been possible for human ingenuity to devise.
Then he went on to say:
Out of these agreements France and Germany may work together in the confidence that can breed peace, instead of the suspicion that can breed war.
Have they not gone far in the Saar agreement? Germany gave up a great deal there in return for what was given up by other nations.
What of Herbert Morrison, the former foreign secretary, who said that this is the only alternative? I return now to the question I asked in all seriousness. Why was article I of part I of the nine power conference agreement worded as follows-I am going to take the time of the house to quote the entire section:
The high contracting parties, members of western European union, take note of and record their agreement with the declaration of the chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany (made in London on 3rd October, 1954, and annexed hereto as annex I) in which the Federal Republic of Germany undertook not to manufacture in its territory atomic, biological and chemical weapons. The types of armaments referred to in this article are defined in annex II. These armaments shall be more closely defined and the definitions brought up to date by the council of western European union.
Why were those words "in its territory" put in the agreement? Does that open the way to the building of armaments in the Saar once the Saar becomes internationalized? There must have been a reason for those words. On the face of them, they appear to leave the door open to the manufacture elsewhere of atomic and other weapons. These are striking words. What was the reason for this qualification? Certainly there must have been much soul-searching before those words were added to an absolute ban that could be lifted only with the unanimous consent to the agreement of the nations.
We ask ourselves, will this agreement turn into bitter disillusionment? We remember

North Atlantic Treaty
the treaty of Rapallo in 1921. We recall the Hitler-Stalin pact of 1939. Will the decisions reached by this agreement ultimately become solutions? Those are questions, Mr. Speaker, that only time can answer. Whatever the answer may be, I believe that in those agreements the free democracies of the west have spoken with a free and united voice rather than in the uncertain babble displayed in the months prior to the defeat of the European defence community.
Will the agreement protect? I cannot believe that France, having suffered from militarism as no other nation has suffered, would have voted approval of the agreement unless she believed that. France knows from personal experience. France feels. France cannot forget. Yet when this question came before the assembly, they voted for it. When properly evaluated, it was a large vote. The vote was 287 to 260, which seems a very insignificant majority for such a tremendously important matter. However, if you count out the 99 communists who could vote only one way, you find that the actual vote of those who were free to vote as they would was 287 to 161. France took the view that failure to approve and adopt these agreements would indeed exact a terrible penalty.
The minister asked, what are the alternatives? That group of communist nations who met in Moscow on December 2 said: Just wait and see. After all, we have discussed this matter for only three and a half years. We have had 16 conferences, I think the minister said, but if we have the opportunity of having just one more, who knows but that we shall establish peace in Europe?
While they talk and prate and counsel "wait and see", they pile up 175 divisions and 80 in the satellite countries. As the minister said, they mobilize in East Germany armed forces to the extent, as I recall it, of 180,000 men.
What are the alternatives? I dislike quoting from what the leaders of other nations have said, but I cannot forget that when this matter was before the British House of Commons Clement Attlee asked in effect: in view of Germany's past actions should she not be disarmed? He answered by saying that it was a logical position, but not a practicable one. Eden said this:
The failure to ratify the pact with West Germany would bring about consequences fearful to predict.
He said also that it would drive Germany once more along dark and dangerous paths. Where is she going if you create a vacuum, a no-man's-land in the centre of Europe? Do you not place that country in a position where, sooner or later, it will fall under communist control?

Sir Winston Churchill saw the danger long before anyone else did. I heard him in the British House of Commons in 1936 when he pointed out that his own party was wrong because they were not mobilizing in the face of rising nazism. I saw Churchill in 1916 when he was in disgrace, when he came back from France wearing the uniform of the armed forces. The house emptied because Churchill was still in disregard, if not disgrace, over Gallipoli. I saw him in the role of a Cassandra in 1936 in the British House of Commons. Yes, he was right then, and others were wrong. We remember Eden when he refused appeasement. Has he changed?
On October 8, at a Conservative party conference, Churchill used these words:
It would be disastrous to the human race to judge the Germans or any other peoples by past crimes committed in their names by dictators. Let Hitler take his name to hell. Let the peoples extend the hand of friendship and forgiveness to each other and walk together through the mysteries of life to freedom, justice and peace.
Scylla and Charybdis agreements are only as strong as the soul and the heart of the nations that enter into them, but the terms impose the greatest control ever imposed on any nation as a result of a conference.
What can Canada do? Well, Canada's contribution to NATO has been an outstanding one. I believe that we must maintain the strength of NATO, and that we should give Canadians a greater opportunity to understand NATO than ever before. Speak to the service clubs and to the public organizations of this country: how many of them have any realization of the responsibilities that NATO imposes upon our country?
I ask the minister this: under this agreement as it now stands, if a number under arms in Germany endeavoured to retrieve their ancestral capital of Berlin and if, as a result, the U.S.S.R. moved in, would we, under the agreement of NATO, find ourselves at war? The minister says no. There are conditions that place a different interpretation upon our responsibilities, qualified as they are in the manner indicated by the minister. I think Canadians as a whole will ask the minister to give that assurance in even more clear and unequivocal terms than he did today.
Believing that NATO should be strengthened, I am one of those who believe-and I speak only for myself in this-that a consultative assembly of NATO parliamentarians from each country might meet from time to time for a discussion and for an exchange of opinions, so that we in Canada would have a fuller realization of our responsibilities in the world of today.

The minister mentioned the contribution of Mr. Dulles of the United States. When and if these agreements are ratified, would it not be an impressive action on the part of the President of the United States if he were to reverse the order of things we have had in the last few years when Sir Winston Churchill has come to America? Because of his position as general commanding the forces of freedom in the last war, he still carries prestige that few possess. Would it not, I say, with the impact of the President's personality and of his persuasive powers, have a tremendous effect if, following the ratification and the approval of these agreements, he were to reverse the order and, himself, go to Great Britain and to France, and give them the reassurance of his presence?
Finally I make this appeal once more to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). It was made today by the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe). Let us, while maintaining these international organizations, be assured as well that our commonwealth will be able to speak with that degree of authority and power that its greater strength, its defences, its development and its economic possibilities will assure. Let us have that opportunity. We are not here to prejudice the Prime Minister, but we do want to have some idea, regarding these international matters affecting Canada and the commonwealth, as to what stands Canada will take before they are taken, rather than after they have become accomplished facts.
And now, fully aware of the dangers inherent in any agreements entered into, I should like to see this parliament, moved as it is by emotions consequent upon two world wars, make a decision with courage, wisdom and infinite compassion. Replete as it may be with danger, it is nevertheless circumscribed in such a way and to such a degree as human ingenuity can make it.
We are going forward. We failed after the first war. We were guilty of withdrawing and leaving Europe isolated. The United States never entered the league of nations. Canada and other nations treated their obligations with almost shameful triviality.
The aim is peace; the means, through strength. We have learned that peace cannot be achieved by chance. This is not an ideal agreement, but we must accept the world as it is. With world conditions as they are, these agreements may not achieve the world of our dreams. But I hope that they can assure a better and a safer world.
How many of us would have thought five years ago that the time would come when an
North Atlantic Treaty
implacable foe would join with us? The minister has said that history is a great teacher. History does teach the fallacy of finality. I believe that, subject to human frailties and human errors, these agreements represent an advance. Perhaps it is old-fashioned to hold this view, but I think the world contest will not be determined by nuclear weapons. I think we need faith. When there is a contest between good and evil, that is important.
Fears we have. For generation after generation men have faced the challenge of freedom. Those without faith have concluded that freedom was about to be destroyed in a glacial avalanche. But faith has always triumphed; and faith will triumph again unless we allow it to die in the grave of doubt and fear. As I see it, this is a step forward to justice under law. It has its dangers. It arouses its fears. But the stakes are high. The failure of this momentous scheme will exact a terrible penalty.
In that spirit, Mr. Speaker, it is the intention of Her Majesty's loyal opposition to support the motion.

Mr. Speaker, the motion moved by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) reads as follows:
Resolved, that it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the protocol to the North Atlantic treaty on the accession of the Federal Republic of Germany, signed by Canada at Paris on October 23, 1954, and that this house do approve the same.
I rise to support the motion. Of course, in saying that, I recognize that hon. members are faced with a decision, in common with the rest of the country, which is not easy to make. I agree with the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he said it is rather regrettable that we had not an opportunity to examine the proposals earlier. I should have liked to see the protocol, and the agreements which are involved in the adoption of this protocol, referred to the committee on external affairs so that there might have been a discussion there, and so that hon. members might have been better informed. Even those of us who have taken the trouble to do a good deal of reading in connection with this matter would still like some of the questions in our minds answered. In a discussion of this kind we are not in committee; we cannot question the minister. All he can do is to reply to the debate. It would have been very much better if these agreements and this protocol could have been referred to the committee on external affairs. That committee could have

North Atlantic Treaty
been set up and perhaps we could have had an examination and the terms of the treaties involved explained to us, and then had the protocol before the house for approval.
As I have said already, I know from personal conversations, both in Canada and abroad, that there are widely held and genuine fears and misgivings concerning the rearmament of Germany. The hon. member for Prince Albert and the minister himself recognize that this is so. Let it not be said that those who conscientiously oppose the proposals are sympathizers either with the communist bloc, because they are so violently opposed to it, or those who are opposed to it are treating what we hope is an emerging democratic Germany as a permanently outcast nation.
I am certain that most members of the house know, as I know, that misgivings are shared by patriotic and peace-loving persons in all parties, in all walks of life and in all the NATO countries. In France, for example, the de Gaullists, the M.R.P., that is the Roman Catholic party, have on the whole bitterly opposed the present proposals for German rearmament, and these are not influenced by the communist party or by communist propaganda.
For my own part, I have given long and anxious thought to the protocol and to the problems of a rearmed Germany under certain conditions and limitations. So have all my colleagues, and I hope that all other hon. members have done likewise.
That we may come to different conclusions may be. a matter of regret, but, certainly, under the circumstances, not unnatural or to be unduly disturbing. For my part, I believe that the best interests of the democratic world will be best served by admitting Western Germany to NATO-that is the purpose of the protocol before us-and then, under the guarantees set forth in the London and Paris agreements, agreeing to the suggested limited and supervised rearmament of the Federal Republic of Germany. But I respect the views of those who arrive at a different conclusion, and those views I hope will be put before the house by my colleagues, perhaps the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
In coming to a conclusion to support the protocol before us, I neither minimize widespread doubts and fears nor misunderstand them. What those of us who support the protocol are doing is to take, as I believe, a worth-while-if calculated-risk.
I said in a previous debate that it was unrealistic to believe that the democratic countries could undertake the defence of
[Mr. Coldwell.l
Western Germany in the event of aggression without the participation of German troops. I said that only within NATO and without establishing an independent German general staff should this be done. I believe the protocol and agreements provide these safeguards. Others may not think they are sufficient. But I do not dispute the contention that there are great risks. There are memories, as the hon. member for Prince Albert said, bitter memories, sharp memories of the horrors of two world wars, provoked by German aggression.
These memories make acceptance of any proposal for German rearmament difficult. But let me remark that the leaders, including the socialist leaders of all the democratic countries which were subjected to devastation and attack, have given public support to this protocol. I should say, lest there be any misunderstanding, that a majority of those attending our convention last summer and our national council more recently were fearful of and opposed to German rearmament before a further attempt had been made to negotiate a satisfactory agreement with Russia on German reunification. That the risks associated with German rearmament are recognized by the sponsors of the proposals is evident in the lengths to which they have- gone to restrict the size of the armed forces Germany may recruit and the weapons she is allowed to manufacture and use. That was quite evident in the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) this afternoon. Those who think that even these are insufficient point *to the former nazis who may be given influential positions in the new German army. That is something that the western powers must watch and resist.
Our preoccupation with aggressive international communism-and it is international and aggressive-must not blind us to the dangers of admitting a sovereign Western Germany into the family of nations. To my mind, however, refusal to do so would cause bitterness and might have the effect of causing them to look behind the iron curtain for support. After all, Germany has looked in that direction before and could do so again, particularly as her economic interests have been largely centred in eastern Europe in the past.
Many who oppose these proposals point this out with the added fear that since Russia alone can satisfy Germany's demand for a revision of her present boundaries, she may, when rearmed, use her stronger international and military position to bargain with the east as well as with the west. That has to be watched.

In 1939 Hitler and Stalin made an unexpected agreement which touched off world war II. We must beware lest the reunification of Germany, the revision of boundaries and German economic interests cause her to take the other side in the cold war if we rebuff her now. Hatred of communism did not prevent the nazis from coming to terms with the soviets in 1939.
Many undoubtedly fear that the safeguards and the pledges made by Herr Adenauer may be ignored by a strengthened Germany which in the past has been and may be again the dominant power in central Europe. Care must be taken that the provisions of the Brussels treaty controlling the level of stocks and the production of armaments as well as the prohibition of atomic weapons, chemical weapons, naval and military aircraft and so on, are not circumvented. I noted the words that were drawn to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Prince Albert, to prohibit the manufacture of these things within Germany's own borders.
For example, our newspapers carried a dispatch on December 9 which said:
The Dornier organization has established a branch in Spain and has built its first aircraft there to get around the ban on Germany's aviation activities.
Many persons reading this doubtless had their opposition to German rearmament considerably strengthened.
Then again many wonder why, if Liddell Hart, General Montgomery and others are correct in stating that atomic weapons and not large armies are now the basis of western defence, the arming of 12 German divisions is so pressing and important. Those who oppose the proposal think that more importance should be given to the effect of rearmament on the future of Germany, the future of Europe and future relations with the Soviet union.
I understand this position and respect it, but my experience at United Nations meetings leads me to believe that world tension has decreased as the western allies have achieved greater unity and strength. That unity and strength must be maintained by the democratic nations.
Fear there is that the rearmament of Germany will result in the irrevocable division of Germany with a revival of the kind of reaction which gave Hitler his opportunity in the 1930's, the kind of reaction there was against the Versailles treaty.
But no proposal for the reunification of Germany on the basis of free elections has been accepted by the Russians. Some believe, quite sincerely, that if pledges were given that a reunited Germany would be a disarmed Germany for a period of time, say ten
North Atlantic Treaty
years, Russia might agree. That proposal might have been made and might have been worth trying but I doubt it would have changed the Russian view. It is too late to suggest it now.
But may I add here that no opportunity for the negotiation of outstanding problems with Russia should be neglected. I was very pleased to note that the minister of external affairs in the course of his speech this afternoon made exactly that point, that even on minor issues, when the opportunity to negotiate settlement occurs, those negotiations should be undertaken in the hope that if we can negotiate some of the minor issues we can ultimately negotiate major ones. If after the ratification of the protocol four-power negotiations are undertaken, we should support them wholeheartedly. I hope and indeed believe that ratification will promote negotiations rather than hinder them.
Perhaps the most potent argument against the proposal is that there is a sharp difference of opinion regarding rearmament in Western Germany itself. The trade unions and the social democratic party are unitedly against it. Those of us who read the reprint of an article from the New York Times in this morning's Montreal Gazette saw that the non-communist youth of Germany met a few days ago and strongly opposed German rearmament. So there is no doubt that there is opposition to rearmament in Germany itself. We must beware lest the sympathies of this large section of German opinion are alienated from the west. They fear a resurgence of militarism as a result of rearmament-hence every precaution must be taken by the supervising authorities to see that the German divisions are organized and officered by men who are entirely free of nazi predilections.
It seems to me, then, that hon. members of this house must weigh risks and advantages and make their decisions on the balance they achieve. This I have tried to do honestly and conscientiously, with the result that, as I said at the very outset, I shall rise in my place and vote for the motion, approving of the protocol.
Many of my friends will arrive at a different conclusion. That I regret, but I can respect their judgment because I understand the basis for their opinions.
The overriding consideration which has governed my own decision may be briefly stated. It is that the failure of Russia to co-operate in the United Nations with a view to setting up the military staff committee, and to participate in the security measures provided for and envisioned in the United Nations charter, made the organization of the regional defensive alliance known as NATO

North Atlantic Treaty necessary and inevitable. I was present at the United Nations when the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) placed the alternative before the United Nations assembly. I approved of what he said at that time and I have not changed my opinion since.
The gradual national disarmament which we envisaged at San Francisco has not been achieved. On the contrary, Russia maintained its armies and strengthened them as we demobilized and turned our airfields back to pastures and our factories to the production of civilian goods. True, a change came over us in 1950 because of the Korean war.
Now the time has come when a proposal is before us for recognition of the partial sovereignty of Germany. As the minister said this afternoon, sovereignty surely involves the right of a nation to defend itself against aggression. How shall that be done?
The alternatives as I see them are to drift along until Germany rearms of her own volition and without supervision or control, or to see her rearmed with the support of one or more friendly powers, perhaps the United States, or to recognize her right to limited rearmament under safeguards and supervision outlined in the treaties. To my mind the limited and supervised rearmament within NATO is the alternative I must support.
The indefinite occupation and defence of Germany by the NATO powers is, of course, another alternative but one which no country is prepared to undertake indefinitely or even in part, without German participation in her own defence.
May I say one further word regarding NATO. I feel very strongly, as I have said so often in the house and wish to reiterate this afternoon, that we in the western alliance would be in a much stronger position in the world if we had paid more attention to article 2 of the NATO agreement. Had we given as much attention to the integration of the economies of the NATO countries as we have to military arrangements, our European allies would have been more stable, more secure against communist infiltration, and this very strength and stability would have minimized the danger of communist aggression against which the NATO treaty was originally formulated. May we take this lesson to heart and in formulating future plans for the maintenance of peace in Europe, Asia and indeed Africa or the rest of the world, give more heed to economic aid as a means of promoting freedom, democracy and world-wide peace and progress.

Mr. Speaker, I must say at the outset that I too look upon this debate as perhaps covering the most important matter to come before


parliament at this session, if not at many other sessions. I listened carefully to the speech given under great difficulties this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) who, by the way, seemed to grow stronger as the minutes passed. For that I was glad. I must say that he presented a sombre picture, one which certainly confirmed my own feelings as to the whole world situation that we face. We are now discussing a matter of tremendous importance, and I believe that each person in this house must look into his own conscience and decide whether or not he has been able to give it adequate consideration. As for me, I have devoted a great many hours of study and contemplation to this whole matter. I have read every single thing that I could get hold of with respect to it in an effort to try to make up my mind on the basis of the fullest knowledge which I was capable of obtaining.
Over the past several weeks, Mr. Speaker, I have noted the intensive campaign of opposition, I must say, carried on by the communists in this and other lands. I must say that, in my judgment, they have overplayed their hands. However, as a result of their overplaying their hands, I believe that a good many serious-minded, loyal citizens of this country have possibly been silenced for fear that they might be classed as communists or communist sympathizers. When I say silenced, I mean in their criticisms, if they have criticisms, of the protocol and the agreements that have been entered into at Paris and London. We in the Social Credit group have all given many hours of study to this complicated group of interrelated protocols, annexes and treaties because it is not easy, in my judgment, to get them all separated and put into their proper perspective so that they can be understood.
The minister's speech this afternoon-and it was an excellent one, I may say-helped us greatly to get a better understanding of this whole complex. But what makes complete understanding much harder to get is the fact that there are so many implications in what was done at both London and Paris. Here we are dealing with matters of power politics, a field in which we can never be quite sure that we have caught the full picture because every move that is made can be understood only against the background of decades of history and against a great many shifting alliances.
In the light of all the complexities and problems associated with the protocol now under discussion, we think that it would have been wiser if the government had brought the resolution before the house so that it

could have been considered in committee of the whole where the members could have asked as many questions as they liked and where they could have made every effort to get a complete understanding of the whole serious situation. However, that has not been done. I do not know what else to suggest to the minister. I know that there are serious misgivings in the minds of many people because we have not brought the protocol in for consideration in such a way that questions can be asked. The only other thing that I could possibly suggest might be reference to the external affairs committee. I would not even do that if it were to be interpreted to mean that what I was seeking was delay, because that is not my object at all. But let us keep in mind the fact that history will judge us with some harshness if it ever takes the view that we have made a decision on this extremely important matter without the fullest possible measure of consideration and study. If the minister can see his way clear to refer this protocol to the external affairs committee for study, I should like to see that course adopted because I would not want anyone to feel that this house took a measure of this great importance and dealt with it summarily without having every opportunity to get at the root of every single thing that a member wants to investigate.
From talking with people and from receiving communications from them I have discovered that a good many of our good, loyal, serious-minded citizens throughout Canada have in their minds many misgivings about the rearmament of Western Germany. Let me hasten to differentiate between the protocol and rearming Western Germany, because there is a difference, in my judgment. I must confess that I have some serious misgivings about the rearmament of Germany myself. The misgivings of serious and good and loyal people in this country revolve around what will really be the result of ratification of the protocol rather than its major purpose. I think that most people feel that the thing that is uppermost in the whole business is the rearming of Germany, with all the possible consequences and dangers that attend that business.
I have received quite a number of communications about the matter. Some I have not placed at a very high level of worth; others I have. I cannot help paying attention to the things that are brought to my attention by people who I know are loyal citizens of this country and are serious-minded people. I have in my hand a letter from one
North Atlantic Treaty
such person; and by the way it is from a man who professes adherence to the Conservative party in my own part of the country. I want to quote from it as being typical of the attitude of quite a number of Canadian people. I propose to read briefly from the letter, Mr. Speaker. I may say that I am quite prepared to table the whole letter if it is desired that I do so. In fact, I will do so anyway because I think this house is entitled, whenever a member quotes from a letter, to see what is in it. This is what this good man says:
It has occurred to me that whereas in a democracy we are all responsible for the actions of our governments it is proper for us to express our opinions when we think they are doing wrong.
I agree with that statement 100 per cent; and I am glad this man had the courage and the anxiety about the whole matter to write to me. He continues:
I am much worried about the rearming of Germany and more particularly our alliance with Germany even though it is only a part of the country. It seems to me to be morally wrong.
We have had no reliable evidence of any repentance on the part of Germany for all that they did, and thus our acceptance of them now really implies condonement of their wickedness. We are being unjust to ourselves and we are failing in a sacred duty to our brothers who were slain by their hands.
No emergency can truly justify saving ourselves at the expense of honour. God always provides a better way if we look for it. Mr. Pearson asked if anyone could suggest a better way. I say let us face the situation squarely as we did after Dunkirk, looking for help neither to right nor to left but only up. In that way only will we be worthy of that help that comes from above
Then in another part of the letter he goes on to say this:
If we do have to come to blows with Russia, which I think we won't, will the acceptance of German help do us any good? I think it will do harm. History has shown that battles are not always won by the side with the biggest army, but by the side with the best will to fight. The will to fight goes with the most righteous cause. We may find many such cases in the Old Testament. Even a dictatorial government must have the will of their people behind them to successfully wage war. We must try to imagine what the feelings of all people of eastern Europe must be in the present case. They undoubtedly will have a horrible memory of German occupation. Our alliance with Germany will associate us in their minds with all that they dread. It will fix their will solidly behind every action that their government takes against us. This I think will more than offset the advantage of having Germany on our side.
I do not wish to quote any more at this time. This man has written me in good faith and said that I might quote from his letter if I wished. I did so because it is typical of of the attitude and feelings of a great many people who are loyal citizens of this country

North Atlantic Treaty
and who can by no stretch of the imagination be called communists or fellow travellers. I say it is typical, and we must not brand these people as communists.
When EDC was being promoted and before France turned it down we were told that the revival and use of the German general staff would not be allowed. That assurance did set some of our very deep misgivings somewhat at rest. But since EDC was scotched and these new proposals were adopted at London and Paris there has been some evidence and quite a good deal of prospect that the German general staff will not only be revived but that members of it will be given a big part to play in rearming Germany. We know that many of them are nazi sympathizers, outright nazis or some other form of extremists, and people generally are fearful that the German general staff, who were mainly responsible for the brutal and bestial acts of the German army during world war II, will soon come to exercise far too much influence not only on military life in Germany but also on the political and social life of the German people as a whole. I think we ought to be given every assurance that this will not be so and that they will not be allowed to do so. What assurances can be given I do not know, but certainly we should be given assurances that they will not be allowed to do so.
I recall that when I visited Germany in 1948 there was an intensive effort going on then on the part of the occupying powers to condition the German people out of their uncommonly strong bent towards militarism and at the same time to encourage and help them to establish a real democracy deep-rooted in their country. These were the two major objectives in the intensive educational campaign that was started by the occupying powers soon after they went into Germany. They realized what a terrific task it would be because for centuries the German people had never taken their individual responsibilities of citizenship. They had let Adolf do it until it became instinctive for them to look for a fuehrer instead of the practice of individual responsibility and taking their fair share in their own government.
Of course the German general staff and the military junta have exercised undue influence over the people since the time of Bismarck, and so it was not surprising to me that for a great time the German people had been developing a national character that leaned heavily toward militarism and war. But during the past ten years the intensive educational campaign of the allies in Germany has taught the younger people to hate militarism and the people as a whole have adopted

democracy as their form of government. It is not deep-rooted, as we know, and perhaps will not be deep-rooted for a good many years. It is quite true it will need a long time to become firmly established, but my opinion is that the younger Germans as a whole bitterly hate even the appearance of a uniform and they have given Theodor Blank, the man who undertook to publicize the new army, a pretty tough time in many areas of the country. In one place I understand they even threw a wine glass in his face when he attempted to speak to them. That is an indication of how they look at it. Does it not seem tragic and ludicrous that we would now turn completely around and plead with the Germans to think in terms of militarism, even if it is limited? It would be especially ludicrous if we did not take every precaution against the revival of the German general staff.
A good deal has been said this afternoon about the dangers involved in German rearmament, and there are dangers. Other speakers have pointed them out. Indeed, the minister himself did so and suggested that in all of these international agreements there is a risk we have to take. I am glad he did not use the term "calculated risk" because a good many people in this country look upon it as more or less a useless term. Certainly any risk is calculated. You never take a risk unless you feel you can get away with it. We know that there are dangers, and I think we should always keep those dangers in mind. If the protocol is ratified, as I hope it will be, then we should never relax in our efforts to prevent the dangers from being realized.
There are dangers we can see and there are dangers that will not become evident for some time after we have begun to gain experience in the practical working out of the protocol. I do not believe I should take the time here to point out too many of these dangers. There are some I shall suggest to which reference may have already been made. A rearmed Germany might try to seize East Germany by force. The minister set some of my misgivings at rest in that regard when he said that there could be no deployment of forces within Germany except at the command of the supreme commander of NATO, which I admit is in itself some control. But still it is not airtight. If a rearmed Western Germany should attempt to seize East Germany by force, thinking perhaps that with the 12 divisions the minister spoke about, the 1,350 airplanes and a naval force of a sort, they would be the strongest military power on the continent with the exception of Russia, what kind of predicament might that plunge us into? That

is the point. It is not whether or not they would be able to accomplish their task, but it would of course intensify the risks of war.
So we have to be very careful to see that there are safeguards against any precipitous action for unification that may be in the minds of a frustrated people who for years have been thinking in terms of unification and who seem to be willing to give their lives for it. I am not one who overlooks the fact that unification of Germany has only been a matter realized in comparatively recent times, and in the long run it is not an important consideration by any means. It is important, but certainly not the most important.
Another rider to this danger might be if the Western German people became frustrated in their desire for reunification and a strong wooing movement on the part of Russia conceivably induced a rearmed Germany to make a deal with Moscow. I wonder what result that might have. We have to look at that possibility. If we had to face a resurgent Germany allied with the imperialist bolsheviks from the east we would of course have our hands more than full, even with NATO.
I might also mention the possibility that ratification might intensify the arms race. That has been suggested, and it is possible, although I do not look upon it as a grave danger by any means. I might suggest, as has already been suggested, that ratification of the protocol might harden the present division of Germany as well as the situation of the east versus the west blocs of the world. It might do that. I do not know. It is something concerning which we have to wait and see. I do not like to think that it will. I hope it will not, but it might put an end to any possibility of achieving success in the drive for disarmament. However, we have to take the risk.
These are the dangers, and there is one other. The complex of protocols, agreements and annexes does set up, I understand, a system of interlocking controls that are expected to operate successfully against the dangers I have mentioned and any others that may be seen. They might work well but it will only be so if all the parties to NATO, the western European union and the Brussels pact continue to act in the very best of faith and if the German people continue to root their democracy deeply, resisting the influence of the German general staff as well as any extremists in other places.
Now, I have faith in Adenauer. So long as Adenauer is there, I think that he could successfully lead Germany along the path of 50433-25
North Atlantic Treaty
rectitude. I believe that, but we must remember that President Adenauer is getting older. Of course, we sincerely hope he will be around a long time to see this thing through. We must not overlook the fact that he is not expected to be around all the time. I am wondering what would happen if the western European nations decided later that it would be wise to raise the ceiling on West Germany's military strength. They could not order an increase; that has to be done voluntarily. I understand that under the treaty the western nations could not force it, they would have to negotiate for it. It is conceivable that in the negotiations Germany might bargain for a relaxation of some of the controls. If a dangerous east-west situation were to arise, a situation of real urgency, the western powers might yield to Germany's desire in order to get the increase.
What would happen then? Away would go the system of controls, and I do not know where it would end. I point these things out, Mr. Speaker, more to indicate what is in the minds of those people who are thinking this thing through very carefully. Certainly a lot of these things were in my mind, although I suppose I must have given thirty or forty hours of study to this whole question since we were told this debate would take place. There are some things that I cannot understand fully even yet, and I suppose a good many people would be in the same position.
As we study this whole complicated series of documents, this protocol, I feel we should do so against the background of two very important things. We should never lose sight of what happened at Munich, and how Munich contributed to the terrible things that eventually took place in world war II. In my judgment it would never do for us to let down our guard for one moment. At the same time, I must say we should do all we possibly can to spread the gospel of love, charity and good will to our fellow men wherever they may be, behind the iron curtain or in front of it.
The second consideration I feel we should always keep in mind is what the bolshevik imperialists are trying to do, and in fact, I think, are determined to do. I believe I understand what it is. I believe that, just as it was true that Hitler and his objectives were made clear by his own publication, "Mein Kampf", today the objectives and determination of the leaders of the bolshevists are made quite clear by the things they do and the documents they publish. Back in 1923, that is a long time ago, Lenin set out a blueprint for communist action over the years. He said;
First we will take eastern Europe, then the masses of Asia, then we will encircle the United States.

North Atlantic Treaty
which will be the last bastion of capitalism. We will not have to attack. It will fall like an overripe fruit into our hands.
We must secure the good will of teachers and professors in schools and universities, of liberal ministers of religion and of the pacifists and reformers of the world in order to create a mental barrage in the minds of the capitalist youth, which shall forever bar them from participating in a carnal conflict with the communist order.
This man Lenin was one of the architects of the communist conspiracy. Coming closer to modern times, I quote a man whom I met at the United Nations, a man by the name of Manuilsky. At one time he was the head of the Comintern and, by the way, was the man who betrayed the Ukraine and led that section into a trap. He said:
War to the hilt between communism and capitalism is inevitable. Today, of course, we are not strong enough to attack. Our time will come in 20 or 30 years.
That is approaching.
To win we shall need the element of surprise. The bourgeoisie will have to be put to sleep. So we shall begin by launching the most spectacular peace movement on record. There will be electrifying overtures and unheard-of concessions. The capitalist countries, stupid and decadent, will rejoice to co-operate in their own destruction. They will leap at another chance to be friends. As soon as their guard is down we shall smash them with our clenched fist.
He was speaking on behalf of the Comintern. What else do we need with that blueprint and the knowledge of events that have been happening in the world since that time and what is happening today? An attempt is being made by the communists now with a bit of a peace movement, overtures and all that sort of thing. We have to beware. That is why I say we have to watch these blueprints very carefully.
A NATO letter for May, 1954, sets out on page 25 a statement showing current Soviet military capacity. I believe the minister described that this afternoon in adequate terms, so I will not need to repeat it. Anyone who wants to see the strength of the communist countries today has only to turn to the NATO letter for May, 1954, page 25, and take a look at it. If you do not get shocked into a sense of reality, then I miss my guess. I should like to ask why in the world Russia has built up such a huge armament in relation to the other parts of the world. Why have her satellites followed suit, as the minister said this afternoon? Why have they allowed Germany to continue divided for all these years? Why have they refused to help bring about a peace treaty for Austria? All these things we have to try to keep in our minds.
I believe fully that the division of Europe was brought about by Russia and her close 
allies through their refusal to take even a good look at suggestions for the reunification of Germany on the basis of free elections, and also because they have constantly refused to co-operate to the smallest extent in trying to solve the many problems that are causing tension in the free world today. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have only a few remarks left, so may I continue and try to conclude before the recess?
Go ahead.

It is clear to me at any rate that Western Germany would not be able to defend herself against an already armed Eastern Germany without having some military strength with which to do it. In addition to that, I feel quite certain that Europe could not possibly defend itself against a possible communist aggression without German manpower and German arms. Just here let me say that in case of trouble between the eastern powers and the western powers, I am sure that the Canadian people would not want Canadian boys to give their lives defending approximately 30 million people who were not taking any part in the responsibility of defending themselves. That is one of the most serious considerations. I feel that such considerations must enter into the minds of the Canadian people from one coast to the other. I would not want that, and I believe I am about average in that respect.
1 believe that the free nations of the world must be strong and be able to withstand the forces that are arrayed against them. I believe that the only thing the communists understand and respect is strength. I feel we have reached a point where we must take a stand to prevent any further communist victories and so that we will not have to continue with any kind of policy of salvage out of our international conferences. We have lost too much already. I think now is the time to take that stand. We have to take it whether or not we want to do so. Perhaps the most important deterrent to communist aggression is the knowledge of the unity of western Europe. For that reason I believe it is wise, very wise, to admit Germany into the North Atlantic community, and I say "the North Atlantic community" rather than NATO, advisedly, and into the western European union.
While I realize that the controls that are set up may not work, I believe there is much less danger to the free world from a possible gradual break-down of controls over a period of years than from a determined adversary sworn to destroy all the free nations of the world, and that maintains a strong fifth column in every country where

they are pledged now to lull the citizens of those countries to sleep with that peace opiate about which I spoke, and who would like to sabotage their efforts to defend themselves if it becomes necessary to resort to armed defence. We do not want to forget quickly how much influence that fifth column had at one time in many countries of Europe, and some that are now far from us.
I am certain in my own mind that NATO has prevented a western push by the communist imperialists before this, and that is why I have supported NATO right from the beginning. And I want my hon. friend who spoke last evening before six o'clock to hear what I am now saying. I say to him, the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon), that I have supported NATO right from the beginning, because I have felt that Canada must be strong, and that Canada must stand with the other free nations of the world to resist communism. I believe we must continue to spend for defence purposes and keep ourselves strong and, certainly so long as the present situation continues, we must give high priority to defence. That is where I stand.
I am glad to hear the hon. member make that statement. As a matter of fact I was going to ask him that question.

I took a note of what the hon. member said last night and I felt that under the circumstances I was obligated to state where I stand. And by the way I am speaking at this time for the Social Credit association of Canada, of which I have the honour to be leader. I am sure all the members of that association, and those affiliated with it, will stand by what I have to say.
The possession by a united west of atomic weapons, and at least a measure of western solidarity, have been I am sure great deterrents. Divided and weak, all the negotiations and peace conferences we could think up would be useless in the face of communist blueprints and determination to reach their goal.
We in this group would like to see a general disarmament. We pray for it and will work for it, but I hope we are not unrealistic enough to believe that we in the free nations of the world, in spite of our great military inferiority under the east, should start disarming unless Russia and her allies give undoubted evidence of their readiness to go along with us in disarmament. I think that we should pursue every effort and take advantage of every possibility to get world-wide agreement on disarmament 50433-254
North Atlantic Treaty
and effective international control of atomic weapons to ensure that they will never be used in war.
If I thought the ratification of the protocol would destroy our chances of achieving general disarmament and effective international control of atomic weapons, I would vote against it, and I would use every ounce of my energy to persuade others to vote against it. But I am convinced that the only thing that will ever bring Russia's communist imperialists seriously to consider disarmament will be the realization on their part that they can never become strong enough to whip us all, if we stand together.
Consequently if we stand together and keep our unity solid and keep ourselves strong, I believe that we will have a much better opportunity, and a much better chance of negotiating for world peace and disarmament, so as to usher in that time for which we all long, the time when "every man may sit under his vine and fig tree and none shall make him afraid." I feel at the present time that we should support the protocol that has been placed before us, give it every possible chance to work, and show unity in the face of the difficult situation which obtains throughout the whole world.
