Mr. Speaker, I have heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) on many occasions in this house when he has given us a review of the international situation, but I do not think I ever heard him to such advantage as I did this afternoon. He was lucid, he was clear and he gave us facts. I think that those facts showed us the motion which is before the Chair and the ratification of this protocol of NATO to be one of the most important pieces of legislation that has ever come before the Canadian parliament. I know he has been suffering from a sore throat, and so on, but he did so well this afternoon that I hope the next time he speaks he has another sore throat. I am not wishing him any harm, but I think the speech he gave and the way he put it when he answered all our fears augurs very well for the future. I cannot help paying this tribute to the speech which he made this afternoon and usually I do not pay compliments.

North Atlantic Treaty
There are two or three things that I want to touch on tonight in regard to this protocol and the questions raised by the speakers this afternoon. After listening to the minister there is not very much a backbencher can say about this protocol. But I think it will be understood that whenever we negotiated with the communists, when we sat down with them, we always did it not being sure of our position and through a sense of weakness, in that the communists had this advantage: they knew that we did not desire war nor did we have any intention of attacking them. But we did not know what they were going to do to us. That gave them an advantage and a great advantage in their negotiations. The result was that many times we came off a bad second. The Geneva conference last summer demonstrated this weakness. I am glad to note that out of this weakness came the realization that if we had continued with any more Genevas we would be placed in such a position that our chances of maintaining peace would be very small indeed.
It was the failure at Geneva and the failure of France to ratify the EDC that awakened people to the sort of danger into which they were drifting. Then Sir Anthony Eden and other statesmen realized it and got together with the people behind them and worked out this protocol which we have before us tonight.
Sometimes out of weakness comes strength. We have been negotiating for years through weakness and it is only when we negotiate through strength that we seem to make any deal with the Russians at all, or make any impression upon them. We have now reached the stage that with NATO we are building up the strength to negotiate. We are in a position to sit down on equal terms with the Russians and negotiate through strength on equal terms. The value of this protocol to me means simply that.
I said that in this house two or three years ago and perhaps I was the first to enunciate the policy of peace through strength. I am convinced-others may have different opinions -that peace never came through weakness and it will never be maintained through weakness. If we are to have peace we must be strong enough to see that we can keep it; therefore tonight we are debating this protocol binding the NATO nations together so that we may negotiate with the communist powers in the future on equal terms.
This afternoon the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) strongly supported the motion before us and raised one or two questions. One of his questions had to do with our troops in Germany and the position in which they would be placed if this new
[Mr. Stick.!
German army took it in their heads to try to get back Berlin. I am not going to try to answer the question for the minister because he is well able to do so himself, as you all know. It was a hypothetical question, of course. But if the German army is to be integrated into NATO, with all the safeguards which were outlined to us this afternoon, I cannot for the life of me see, from a military standpoint, how the German army on its own is ever going to take Berlin without orders from the supreme commander of NATO.
The question was also raised: what is the position of the Canadian troops under this arrangement if they do not get sufficient safeguards? Well, if I know the Canadian troops and the spirit of the fighting qualities of the Canadian troops, I do know this: If *a fracas takes place in Europe, they are not going to sit on the sidelines; they are going to take part in it. That is what they are there for. There are under this protocol risks which we have to take. There is no treaty today, however much you may bind it with safeguards, that is going to be kept unless the will behind it is to keep it. It has been demonstrated often enough in the last five or six years that treaties are kept by certain powers only when it is convenient for them to keep them. We therefore must accept certain risks when we ratify this protocol. There has never yet been an airtight treaty, Mr. Speaker, so my position tonight is to rise and support this protocol, fully accepting the risks which I know I have to take. I am sorry I have to ratify it, but because we have no choice I ratify it and am going to vote for it, for this very simple reason. The general welfare of this country is wrapped up in this treaty, and possibly the peace of the world.
When the hon. member for Prince Albert emphasized the importance of this protocol coming before this parliament and the duty of each member of this parliament toward the treaty, he brought out a very good point. It is the duty of hon. members to safeguard the welfare of the people of this nation and to try to maintain peace. That is why I am supporting it, with all its drawbacks and with all its risks.
I am going to support the protocol, Mr. Speaker, because I am here to safeguard the general welfare of the people of Canada and to try to maintain peace. That is why I am going to vote for it and that is why I hope all hon. members will make up their minds on that basis and not on the basis of party. This is beyond party. It is the national welfare that is before us, and if we vote on that basis there will be no doubt of this

protocol being ratified in an overwhelming manner. I am voting for it for the reasons I have stated.
I do not want to take any more time because I know many hon. members want to express their thoughts. I simply wanted to express mine and to say once more that in voting for this treaty I am voting on behalf of the general welfare of the people of Canada and for the peace of the world.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to confine my remarks this evening to the aspect of this problem referring to the rearmament of Germany. If my remarks should savour somewhat of a military appreciation, you, sir, know my background, and I have no apologies to make.
As has been stated on several occasions during the debate already, it is not unnatural that many people view with apprehension the rearming of Germany. The wounds inflicted during world war I and world war II left deep impressions in the hearts and homes of thousands of Canadians. These wounds are not yet healed. On the other hand, it would be senseless for us deliberately to keep open the scars and to continue the hatreds cultivated during the war years. It is difficult for the ordinary mortal to follow the divine injunction to love one's enemies, but if what we choose to call common sense indicates a similar course then perhaps we may be capable of rising slightly above the implications and emotions of frail human nature.
The fears which have been expressed might, I think, have been to a certain extent relieved had it been possible for the government to have given an opportunity for a full discussion on this problem before this. But, even now, I will endeavour to remove some of those fears which beset the people of Canada. In order that we may have a correct approach I will review quite briefly the events surrounding the background of this problem.
You will remember that during the period of happy optimism which followed immediately after the cessation of hostilities at the end of world war II, the hope expressed at Potsdam persisted for a short time that the German people might remain unarmed for many years because all the great states adjacent to the reich were on seemingly good terms so that the chances of war in Europe were regarded as remote.
It was not until the four-power pact of 1946 failed in the face of the Russian demand for the control of the Ruhr that the western
North Atlantic Treaty
powers found it necessary to build up the economic life in their respective spheres of Germany in order that they might relieve the burden on their own taxpayers. From that date on the division of Germany became more and more clearly defined and we also witnessed the miracle of West German resurgence.
Then followed the Soviet rejection of the Marshall plan, the Czech-communist coup of 1943, and the Russian blockade of Berlin countered by the airlift on the part of the western powers. These events eventually drove the western powers in self-defence into the Atlantic alliance. Even then no serious consideration was given to the creation of any German contingents although it was known that Russia had equipped the police forces of Eastern Germany with tanks, artillery and modern arms at that time. Therefore the blame for the failure of the Potsdam agreement lies squarely on the shoulders of the U.S.S.R. It was not until operations were started in Korea in 1950 that Europe really became alarmed. The fear that an invasion similar to that which took place in South Korea might be launched in central Europe became great, that is an invasion by proxy. It was then and only then that Mr. Winston Churchill, as he then was, advanced a suggestion to the council of Europe that West German troops might be integrated into the defence system of NATO.
The various plans which culminated in the European defence council failed to materialize after the rejection of that European defence council by the French chamber last year because of its supra-national character. Now, it seems to me that the west has but three choices. I put these three choices in slightly different language to that voiced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) this afternoon.
The first choice is to act on the assumption that Russia will never attack through West Germany and therefore we can leave the Germans unarmed and undefended. In other words, let us turn back the clock to the Potsdam period. That is just not practical- you cannot turn clocks back.
Secondly, to assume full responsibility for the entire defence of West Germany by the western powers. The adoption of such a policy would mean much heavier commitments in arms, money and manpower by the western powers. In order that Canada might bear her full share of any such program she might easily be asked to station a much larger force in Europe than the one brigade we have stationed over there at the present time.

North Atlantic Treaty
I do not think that anyone suggests seriously that Germany could be occupied indefinitely by the allied forces. It would be repugnant to all the principles of democracy. Such an idea would be politically impossible and furthermore could easily ruin the economy of the western powers.
The third alternative that it has been suggested we adopt is to give West Germany the opportunity to contribute to the maintenance of the forces now being built up by the NATO powers in the hope that those forces will be sufficiently strong to deter Russia from committing any overt act which would lead to war.
The choice really lies between linking the federal republic of West Germany strongly with the west or allowing her to drift about in the centre of Europe, eventually and inevitably to be sucked into the Soviet system.
I think a neutral and defenceless Germany simply does not make sense. The days when any country could remain in splendid isolation are, I think, past forever.
It seems to me that the question we must ask ourselves is whether we really need a German contribution in order to offer a strong deterrent to possible Russian aggression. I am fully aware of the risks we run by rearming Germany. Is it possible for the west to prevent war without German manpower? That is the question I ask.
A few years ago General Eisenhower said that German manpower was essential to stop Russia from overrunning western Europe. Up to now German manpower has not been available, nor have the Russians attacked in western Europe and overrun western Europe. Why is this? The answer to that question is that up to now we have held the lead with the atomic bomb. But today the Russians, too, have the atomic bomb.
So before answering my question as to whether we really need German forces I think we should assess the opposing forces as we know them to be.
From the most reliable information available it is indicated that the U.S.S.R., Eastern Germany and the eastern European satellite states today have over six million men under arms, of which number four and a half million approximately are in the army. Mr. Harold Macmillan, the minister of defence in the British house, on November 18 during the debate on a motion similar to this one, stated that well over 100 divisions could be made available by the Russians in 30 days and that their total forces numbered over 400 divisions. More than one-third of these Soviet divisions are tank or mechanized divisions armed with modern equipment. Russian tanks today stand on the line of the

Elbe. They dominate the central plains of Germany and within a few hours' run could be on the Rhine.
The precise figures given for the forces of the western powers have not been made public, but the figure which is generally accepted is a little short of 50 divisions, with another 50 divisions in reserve. That, Mr. Speaker, is the measure of our disadvantage. Surely another 12 divisions from West Germany will help us to offset that disadvantage. The Soviet air force seems to have been stabilized in the last few years to a figure of about 20,000 aircraft of which more than half are modern jet types. Perhaps half that number of aircraft are available under the command of the supreme allied commander of the European forces. The German contingent is limited to 1,350 aircraft of which I understand some 10 units are to be of tactical bombers and 4 units are to be fighters, while the other 2 units are to be made up of reconnaissance aircraft. I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made a slip of the tongue this afternoon when he said they were all fighters.
The Russian navy comprises some 20 to 25 cruisers, 100 to 150 destroyers and at least 350 submarines. I think the navies of the west are at least as strong as that. However, with regard to this problem we are dealing particularly with armies and air forces.
There is little doubt that the Soviets have stockpiles of atomic and thermonuclear bombs. It is, however, by no means certain that the Russians would use those terrible weapons at the commencement of any aggressive action that they might plan; for there is no real defence against strategic forces armed with H-bombs. The western powers also have their long-range bombers widely distributed throughout more than 150 airfields in Europe and Africa, all within bombing range of the principal Russian cities and their principal centres of communications. Since both sides have many airfields from which their bombers, armed with H-bombs and A-bombs, - might take off, I therefore suggest that it would be the wildest gamble for either side to count upon its ability to knock out or to neutralize the other's power to retaliate. A war fought with H-bombs could only result in mutual destruction of the nations concerned. Both sides may therefore hesitate to use the H-bomb, in much the same manner as both sides in world war II refrained from using poison gas.
The large Soviet forces with more or less conventional arms to which I have already referred, however, constitute a threat if we do not possess a deterrent; and I do not see

how we can rely solely upon a weapon such as the H-bomb which quite possibly we might never dare to use. We are therefore obliged to provide ourselves with the means of defeating, with conventional arms, an attack by conventional arms as well as retaining the power to retaliate against thermonuclear attack. By maintaining powerful and conventional forces armed with modern weapons for use in the field, the NATO powers hope to deter the Soviet from using their armies.
We have been told over and over again that the west does not have sufficient manpower to provide an effective deterrent against the Russian armies without a contribution from Western Germany. Furthermore, if war broke out, whatever might be the final outcome Western Germany would be the first country to suffer. All the cities of the Ruhr are within range of rockets of the V-l or V-2 type now in positions occupied by the Russians today. In short, western Europe and Great Britain cannot be defended without including in their defensive zone the territory of West Germany. It therefore surely makes sense for us to defend West German territory and to have that defence provided with rather than without the assistance of West German manpower.
A great many people from one end of Canada to the other are apprehensive, as I have already said, about rearming Germany and they have expressed great anxiety over the steps which are now being taken. Many fear that the German army, once formed, may get out of hand. These fears exist in West Germany itself. As has already been done by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), may I call attention to the safeguards which are included in this agreement. While EDC sought a complete surrender of national sovereignty to a supra-national organization and was rejected on that score, the new plan still demands a partial surrender of sovereignty by all western powers. The maximum size of the armies and air forces of all powers is laid down. For Germany, as we have already been told, the forces laid down are 12 divisions, 1,350 aircraft and a navy designed solely for coastal patrol. Only by unanimous vote of NATO can these forces be increased. Another safeguard is this. So far as is practical, these forces are to be interlocked. The degree of their integration is to be left to the supreme allied commander in Europe. But the important feature of that integration will be the allotment of German staff officers to the supreme headquarters so that those staff officers will be in constant touch with the thoughts, opinions and philosophy of the
North Atlantic Treaty
allied staff officers. I believe that a great responsibility will be placed upon the staff officers of the western powers, including Canada, who will be serving on that headquarters staff, to imbue the officers of the German general staff with the spirit of the proper position of an army in a democracy.
The forces will be allocated and deployed under instructions from the supreme allied commander. Once deployed they cannot have their positions changed or be redistributed by any national authority without the consent of the supreme allied commander. As has already been said this afternoon, Germany cannot manufacture in her own territory atomic, biological or chemical weapons, nor make certain other types of weapons, except on the recommendation of the supreme allied commander. He also has control of the supply of petrol and so forth, the so-called logistic support as described in the articles of the agreement.
NATO is also provided with the authority to conduct rigid inspections. But probably one of the best safeguards in keeping the German army within its proper sphere of activity is the feeling that exists among the people of West Germany themselves as to the relation of their army to the state. There is by no means a unanimous desire on the part of the Germans to make a contribution to the common effort. The main argument upon which this reluctance is based is not dissimilar to the fears held by many people outside of Germany and in this country. I think the first and foremost one is based upon the traditional position held by the German army in German politics during the past century. Hon. members who have read "The Nemesis of Power" by Mr. Wheeler-Bennett will realize the political influence which was in the past and might in the future be exercised by a German army on German foreign policy.
There is an old saying that Prussia was not a country with an army but an army which ran a country. The question which is now being asked both inside and outside of Germany is: Can a German democracy exist side by side with a German army? Under Kaiser Wilhelm II and under Hitler it could not. Nor could it exist under the regime of the Weimar republic. Under Kaiser Wilhelm and under Hitler no democracy existed in Germany. During the days of the Weimar republic the army, by the sheer strength of the personality of the army commander, dominated the foreign policy of that republic. The question asked is: Will conditions be different now? I am pleased to say that western statesmen believe that they will be.
In the first place, Germany today is divided. I think we hope, in exactly the same

North Atlantic Treaty
way as Germany aspires, that eventually some day, perhaps in the quite distant future, Germany once again will be united when it is possible for the German people to express their desire freely as to the type of government which they desire. However, Germany is divided today and we notice that the more warlike Prussian states and Pomerania are in East Germany. They are already armed. The more democratically-minded and peaceful peoples of Hanover, Schleswig-Holstein, Hesse, the Rhineland states and Bavaria form the great majority of the inhabitants of the federal republic.
Furthermore, Germany will have a democratic constitution at the same time as she will have an army based on compulsory military service. During the days of the Kaiser and of Hitler they had an army based on compulsory military service but they did not have a democratic government. The new German army will be a conscript army and it will be controlled by a parliament alive to the dangers of the political influence of the army in the past. It will be very close to the army because, as I have said, the army will be a conscript army drawn from the youth of the country in all walks of life.
If I may digress for a moment, I think it would be of interest for us to look at the personalities who are at present controlling or will in the near future control that army. At the head of the organization will be Theodor Blank, director of the federal German office of security and defence, which is similar to our Department of National Defence. Herr Blank very recently stated:
The only man who can be entrusted with the defence of a system is the man who believes in it.
Thus, writes the special correspondent of the Manchester Guardian on Thursday, January 13, 1955, Herr Blank "has summed up his determination to make sure that the new German soldier should be regarded as a citizen in uniform." How very different that philosophy is to that of the old Prussian regime. Herr Blank has been appointed by Chancellor Adenauer to head the shadow ministry of defence in the federal republic of West Germany. He is a former trade union leader and is a member of the Christian Democratic party. The army officers who have been mentioned prominently in the German press as the most likely leaders of the West German army are first of all General Ludwig Cruewell, a Rhinelander, not a Prussian, who hails from the Ruhr valley. He was born at Dortmund in 1892. He was not a professional soldier. He was educated at the universities of Grenoble and Munich. In fact he had a comparatively short military career before he was captured in Africa on the 1st of June, 1942, and he re-
[Mr. Pearkes.l
mained as a prisoner of war until the end of the war. Press reports indicate that he will be the commanding general of the new German army.
The other name that is prominently mentioned, and is perhaps better known, is that of General Hans Speidel, who was chief of staff to Field Marshal Rommel in army group B. He is mentioned as being the chief of the German delegation to NATO. He is not a Prussian. He is a Wurttemberger, born in 1897. These men, as I have said, are not Prussians, nor did they at any time hold any blind unreasoning devotion to the nazi regime. In fact, Speidel risked his life to free Germany from nazi tyranny through his connections with Rommel and the revolt against Hitler. If the government of the federal republic therefore enforces its constitutional authority, the army will not be in a position to usurp that authority. There would seem little doubt in my mind that Herr Blank, who is responsible for the build-up of the German army, has any illusions on the dangers that exist.
I believe that here is a place in which Canada, the western powers, the Canadian officers and the officers of the western powers stationed in Germany have an important role to carry out. They could explain to the new German army the right position which any army occupies in the organization of any democratic state. Again, I feel it will depend on the attitude which is taken by the Deuts-chen Soldaten Bund, that is the German exservicemen's league. Will these men confine their activities, as the branches of our Canadian Legion do, to looking after the welfare of their old comrades or will they advocate the erection of some new military caste? These men have fought one or two wars, and many of them through both. I cannot believe that even our late enemies will want to see the creation of a military caste again.
On the other hand, as opposed to the possible attitude of these veterans, there is a strong element of pacifism existing in Germany today which is not likely to permit the new army to get out of hand. There are so many visible reminders in Germany, and I have seen them myself, of the price Germany paid that it is not surprising that strong elements of emotional pacifism exist in practically all social groups in Germany today. I should like to read a brief quotation from the special correspondent of the Manchester Guardian Weekly, which appeared under date of Thursday, January 13, of this year when he was discussing West German defence and democracy. He says:
One favourable factor is the difference of outlook between young Germans and the older generation. Most observers would probably agree that

the young Germans who have grown up during and since the destruction of the nazi regime present one of the most heartening features in the country. They are open-minded and are far more sensible and realistic than one had reason to expect. They are certainly not inclined to submit to indoctrination or to accept authority as blindly as their elders have done.
Therefore, in spite of all the powerful arguments which may be advanced against German rearmament, I feel forced to recognize the necessity for a German contribution towards western defence. As stated by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker), with the other members in this party I will support the resolution which has been placed before us by the government. I have reached that decision, not with enthusiasm but as the choice of a lesser evil. I recognize the risks involved, not only to the free institutions of Western Germany itself, but also to the peace of the world, should the German army at some far distant date be in a position to make war contrary to the wishes of the North Atlantic powers. But I have to be realistic. I cannot see a force of 12 divisions launching an offensive against 100 Russian divisions. It does not make sense to me. I am not elated at the prospect of seeing this field grey army once again in existence. But if the participation of Germany in the western European union will make that system effective, I am prepared to accept the risks. I believe we all pray that there will be no war. Just because we offer prayers, however, we are not absolved from the responsibility of taking whatever action we can to ensure that there is no war.
In conclusion, I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to give us a little more information regarding the precise position of the Canadian forces now in Europe. The United Kingdom, as is well known, has made a commitment of four divisions and their second tactical air force. She is also very heavily committed financially. Just what is the status of the Canadian brigade and the air division in Europe? The minister referred to it today, but we do know that for operational and training purposes heretofore the Canadian brigade has been under the command of the British commander on the Rhine. We are vitally interested in this problem. Any further explanation that he can give us regarding the system of command would be beneficial to the country.
We have heard of the increases and further commitments which have been made by the government of the United Kingdom. This afternoon the minister said he had given assurance that Canada would play her full part in the new defence organization. Is he satisfied that Canada is playing her full part in relation to what the other NATO powers
North Atlantic Treaty
are doing? While he has made no commitment to the other powers as to whether Canada is to give any guarantee that her forces will remain in Europe for any definite period or whether there is to be any increase in these forces, perhaps he would inform this house as to whether it is the intention of the government to make any further commitments in that respect.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
In rising at this time, Mr. Speaker, I am deeply conscious of that sense of appreciation which I am sure is often felt by every member of this House of Commons. Differ though we may on major or minor issues-and we now have before us one of major importance-all of us are extremely grateful for the fact that we in this country are the proud possessors of free institutions including, in particular, this free parliament, where it is not only our right but our obligation to express our firm convictions. That, Mr. Speaker, is what other members taking part in this debate are doing, members from all sides of the house, and that is what I propose to do at this time.
As my leader the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) indicated this afternoon I would do, I rise at this time to oppose the motion. I do so, Mr. Speaker, for three reasons. First of all, I shall register my opposition from a deep personal conviction. It is my judgment that the rearming of Western Germany at this time is a step we should not now be taking. My second reason for rising to express this opposition is that I am satisfied, as other members are-indeed as other members have said-that there are thousands of good, solid, patriotic Canadians -never mind the others-from one end of this country to the other who are concerned about this step. Indeed there are many who feel it should not be taken,, and I believe their view should be expressed in this debate as early as possible.
I also take this position because, as my leader pointed out this afternoon, it is the position of the movement to which 24 of us in this house have the honour to belong. As my leader pointed out, at our national convention in August 1954 a decision was taken against the rearming of Western Germany at this time.
Further, as my leader pointed out in his address this afternoon, the matter was under very serious consideration at a meeting of our national council this past week-end. That meeting of course was held with the knowledge of the debate to be undertaken in the house this week; and the view of that council by majority vote was that we should oppose the rearmament of Western Germany at this 50433-26

North Atlantic Treaty
time. And so I say it is for those three reasons I rise now to state my opposition to the motion presented to the house this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson).
All of us recognize, and that recognition has been stated by every member who has spoken, that this is a very difficult question-perhaps the most difficult one that most members in this present parliament have had to face. Everyone will agree that, at best, the proposal to rearm Western Germany at this time is a calculated risk fraught with very real danger. Indeed the Secretary of State for External Affairs said this afternoon that at best it had to be regarded as a tragic necessity.
A while ago the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick), in indicating that he would vote for the motion, said, if I heard him correctly, that he was sorry that he had to vote for it, but he felt from conviction that he had to do so. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes), who has just spoken, expressed similar sentiments.
In other words everyone recognizes that the risk being taken is fraught with danger. Those who support the taking of that risk feel that it has to be taken because of the menace of Soviet imperialism. Some of us feel that it is precisely because of that menace-and it is a menace-and that it is precisely because of the seriousness of the world situation at this time, and that it is precisely because the division of our world into two camps should not be pushed beyond the point of no return, that Western Germany should not now be rearmed.
I wish to say very clearly that I do not impute to any of those in the house who support this motion any militaristic or warmongering motives, and I abhor the fact that there are in this country those who do impute such motives. That is not the way to deal with an issue of this kind. There are too many members in the House of Commons who, themselves, have suffered at the hands of German militarism for anyone to think that there is any member in the house who likes the idea of putting arms back into the hands of Germans.
We in the House of Commons, and the people of this country from coast to coast, will never forget the names Dachau, Buchen-wald and Belsen. We will never forget those six million Jews who were slaughtered during the Hitler regime in Germany, an awful blot not just on those who perpetrated such a crime but on our times. There is no doubt about it that no one, not even the most ardent advocate of the motion before

us, wishes to put arms back into the hands of the Germans. Those who are making the decision to vote for the motion are doing so as a result of applying their best judgment to the problem, because they feel it is the best way out of a dilemma and the best solution of some of the most difficult problems now confronting the world.
By the same token I ask that no one say of anyone in any corner of the house who rises to oppose the motion that he is a communist stooge, that he is playing the communist game, either wittingly or unwittingly, or that he is trying to undermine the strength of the west, or that he is unwilling to take steps to bring Germany back into the family of nations. Thank God, Mr. Speaker, we have a parliament where we can discuss these issues on their merits.
I have been delighted at the level of debate thus far, even though I disagree with the conclusions reached. I have listened with deep respect to the arguments put forth and I rise confident that, though my position may be different from any that has been expressed thus far today, the same respect will be shown for my position which, as I say, I believe is shared by a great many people in this country.
What we are seeking to do is to bring to bear on the problem before us the results of our best judgment. It is my judgment that the position taken by the movement to which I belong, at its national convention and national council, is the correct one, and that we should not rearm Germany at this time.
Not only is the question in itself a difficult one, fraught as it is with memories and emotions, and all the rest of it, but it is a difficult and tangled question procedurally. So far as most of us are concerned, so far as the people of Canada who are watching this debate are concerned, this is a debate on German rearmament. The Secretary of State for External Affairs could point out that that is not the motion he has proposed, but that he is proposing a motion for the approval of a protocol admitting the Federal Republic of Germany to NATO.
He will readily admit of course that the rearmament of Germany is involved in the other agreements to which he referred this afternoon; so that in fact, tangled though it is, we do have involved in the proposition that is before us the fundamental question of German rearmament.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, if I may say so with deep respect, I think confused that issue this afternoon by having quite so much to say about the right of a free and democratic Germany to be brought

into the western community. I agree with that and I want it to take place, but the difficulty that confronts us is that what we have before us is not just a motion that German sovereignty be restored; that Germany be brought into the orbit of the west. We are confronted with a multiple proposition, including some things that are good, but including this one element which some of us feel is exceedingly dangerous. Because of that one element, the proposal to agree now to the rearmament of Germany at this time, I for one cannot support the motion. My vote, Mr. Speaker, which will be against the motion presented to the house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, will be a vote on my own behalf and on behalf, I believe, of many thousands of Canadians against rearming Germany at this time.
Since I have taken that position the obligation rests upon me to say why I think this step should not be taken, particularly in view of the well-thought-out arguments that have been presented by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and by others, including the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) who just preceded me with an analysis of the whole situation from a military point of view.
I think everyone will recognize that basically my reason-and I am sure that goes for others in the house who no doubt will join with me in opposing the motion-is that some of us have come to the conclusion that in view of the type of armaments that are available for modern warfare we simply cannot permit the world to go to war again. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich dares to hope that the hydrogen bomb is so terrible that it will not be used; therefore we must have conventional armaments upon which to rely. We all hope that is true, but I wonder whether in our heart of hearts any of us really believes that a third world war would go very long without the use not just of the now obsolete atomic bomb but of thermonuclear weapons. No, Mr. Speaker, I feel we have to start from that premise and somehow we must take the kind of steps which will make sure that war will not break out again.
I liked the challenge the Secretary of State for External Affairs threw out this afternoon -often when he makes speeches with the conclusions of which I do not agree I find that they nevertheless contain many sentences I enjoy, sentences that get quoted by those of us in this group-I liked the challenge he threw out when he suggested that it is up to us in this day and age to see that the tremendous forces and powers that are being given to us by science are used not for warfare but for welfare. It is no longer 50433-26^
North Atlantic Treaty
a dream, no longer something we must hope for. It has become a necessity for us to do so. If we use these things for welfare, we are blessed with a glorious future. If we use them for warfare there is no future.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, starting from that basic position that we must expect a third world war to result in the possible end of civilization, so that it is to be avoided if at all possible, I come to the immediate question as to whether or not Western Germany should be rearmed. I feel it should not be rearmed because by doing so we run a greater risk of war breaking out than would otherwise be the case. I see that greater risk in two ways. Gn the one hand, I frankly admit that I am afraid, as are a great many people, of what a rearmed Germany herself may do.
I congratulate those who devised the controls that are written into the agreements that are behind the motion before us. They are the most effective controls of that kind we have ever seen. I recognize the statements that have been made by others, that for the first time there is a Germany in which the political arm will be superior to the military. But, Mr. Speaker, we are not far enough away from what the Germans have done in two world wars to be sure the same military aggressiveness that broke through the controls, lesser though they were, which were set up after world war I, will not break through again. One thinks of the complications that arise because of the various ways in which changes can be made. Some things can be changed only by unanimous consent; some things can be changed only by a two-thirds majority, and some things can be changed by a simple majority. Some of the controls are simply guarantees based on the pledge of the present German chancellor, Dr. Adenauer. When one realizes that in all these things are certain economic compulsions, he realizes that those controls, strong though they are, well worked out though they are, can be broken through.
My leader this afternoon quoted that dispatch from Reuters concerning the Dornier organization which has already established a branch in Spain for the production of aircraft to get around the prohibition of manufacture of that type of aircraft in Germany itself. We know the ingenuity of these people. The fact of the matter is that though certain non-Prussians, as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich said, may in the immediate future be in high positions in the German army, they will have to rely on men who had military experience in world war II. I suggest that there is very real danger that it will not be long until those same people will again be in charge of

North Atlantic Treaty
German troops, with all the compulsions, the compulsion particularly toward German unification, that are there. I need not drive home the point that the danger is very real.
As for German unification, I do not want to misquote the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I believe he said this afternoon that would of necessity or inevitably be a major factor in German policy, the desire to reunite the two parts of that country of so many millions of people. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, because of these underlying compulsions, it is my fear, and the fear of a good many people, that we might find in the not far distant future we would ourselves be the pawns of the militarists who have been our enemies in two world wars. Remember that it will not be long under this arrangement until the German military people will be the largest single group in the European continental part of NATO. They will be newcomers. They are like the new members in the back row of this house; it does not take long for new members to get down to the front. It will not be long before this newcomer to the North Atlantic partnership will have a major voice because of its strength on the continent of Europe. I suggest we have to think very carefully before we agree to the arming of Germany at this time.
As I said earlier, and as my leader said this afternoon, those of us who take this view must not be regarded as opposed to the idea of bringing Germany back into the family of nations. I would go further than bringing her back into the western group; I look forward to the day when Germany might be able to take her place in the United Nations, and to the day when that organization might be enlarged to take in all the nations of the world. I know there are those who will say "There is a dreamer", but I submit that in the light of thermonuclear warfare the dreamers have become the realists. There is no future unless we get rid of war itself.
As I said earlier, the rearming of Western Germany would increase the danger of war rather than decrease it on two counts. My first point was that I would be afraid of what would be done by a rearmed Germany herself. My second point is that this step will increase the danger of war, because, if I may use the very language the minister used this afternoon in trying to set the argument aside, it is in the nature of an irrevocable step in the further division between east and west. I know that east and west are divided; I know that the Soviet union has played a major part in bringing about that division, not only in drawing the line of division but pushing it as far west as she can.


I know how obstinate the Soviet union has been; I know too that one must not think of West Germany as far as we are concerned as being any different in a military sense than the placing of arms in France or any other of the NATO countries. But let us face the fact that this has become a fetish; this has become a point which seems to the other side to be a case of our taking an offensive step.
There is no question, no matter what our philosophical views of war and peace may be, that we are in the kind of world where you have to be in the position to negotiate from strength. But there are two kinds of strength; there is not only military strength, but moral strength. As for military strength I listened with interest to the exposition made by the hon. member who preceded me as he made the point that from the military point of view we need the extra 12 divisions and extra German aircraft in order to achieve a balance. Suppose that takes place and that so-called balance is achieved. Is that the end of it or does the other side then decide it has to get more? Then where do we go from there? Is Spain next? I hope not. I hope there is some point where we will realize that we in the west not only need military strength but that we need moral strength.
I think that our moral strength is weakened if we at this time put arms into the hands of ex-nazis. I want the west to be strong. I accept the proposition, whether I like it or not, that in the world today we have to be in a position to negotiate from strength; but I think there comes a point where you will push that building of strength beyond the point of no return, where there is nothing left but an arms race which can have only one end, an explosion into a catastrophe that can mean the end of civilization.
I believe that in this world today we are playing for time. We need it terribly. There are things that we can do if we are given the time. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, as I have already suggested, referred to the tremendous forces being made available to us as science gets down to the power of the atom with its tremendous peacetime uses. If we had the time I think mankind could yet turn this world from one of recurring wars to one of permanent peace and human accord, with a high standard of living for mankind the world over.
I think we can yet achieve the dreams of the religionists and poets of days gone by, yes our own dreams and hopes, but we need time. Let me get specific rather than poetic. We need time to push the Colombo plan, and to push it a lot more than the Secretary of State for External Affairs is proposing that we

push it by increasing our contribution by only a million dollars. We need time for tremendous advances on the economic front.
This afternoon the minister mentioned the need for solving the basic causes of war, for getting down to the roots of things. We need time for that. If we had the time 1 think we can do it. Given the time I think we can remove some of the causes of the world's ills. We can change the picture so that instead of two-thirds of the world's people going to bed hungry tonight, as they do every night of their lives, there might be some sharing of the food and good things that we can produce.
We need time for these things. My fear is that if we take the wrong step we may throw time away. We need time for further diplomatic efforts. This afternoon the minister said, in response to the suggestion that still further efforts should be made to get together with the Soviet union to solve the problem of Germany, that sixteen attempts had been made during the last several years. The inference was this: Is it fair to ask for another attempt to be made?
I would rather that we made 16 more attempts than go to war. Almost everybody who ever discusses the United Nations when some heated discussion is going on says that it is far better that they should be calling each other names and fighting with words than that we go into the catastrophe of a hot war.
I think we should continue the efforts to obtain the reunification of Germany even if it does mean multiplying the efforts and multiplying the attempts. I was going to say, multiplying them times without number.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs suggested this afternoon that one of the cornerstones of German policy will be the reunification of that country. He talked about giving Germany sovereignty. Even this set of agreements does not give her complete sovereignty. So far as military matters are concerned she surrenders sovereignty in the same sense that France and other nations in the agreement do, but in addition she has no sovereignty over her relations with East Germany or in the making of peace with her enemies in the last war.
So the German problem is still there. It is not solved by the arrangements that are now suggested. I think the Ottawa Citizen is right in its editorials when it suggests that the possibility of negotiating the reunification of Germany after we have armed West Germany is not as good as it would be
North Atlantic Treaty
if we were not to take that step, which I am afraid is going beyond the point of no return.
So I urge in all seriousness and in all earnestness that the house give a great deal of consideration to this matter. It may be said, and said rightly, that whichever step we take we will really never know whether we are right or whether the other step should have been taken. Of course, if we take the wrong step, whichever one it is, and the result is a third world war with all its catastrophic consequences, it will be known that it was wrong only if there is anyone left to know it. Let us avoid that situation, Mr. Speaker. Let us use the time we have to push for the settlement of disputes along the lines outlined in the charter of the United Nations. Let us use the time we have to get the rest of the world into that world organization. Let us pursue our economic attacks on the problems connected with war. Let us try to remove the causes of war. We have time to do these things. Let us not throw away our opportunity by taking the wrong step.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I said that I rose to make these remarks particularly conscious of the great possession that is ours in this free parliament, in which we have not only the right but the obligation to express our convictions and what we believe to be the convictions of the people who sent us here. Having been able to make these remarks without some of the interruptions that I thought might come, I now want to express my appreciation of the respect that has been shown for my views by those hon. members who I know do not share them. I trust that the debate will go on in that vein and that we shall have discussion of this important question on the basis that it is our job to bring our best judgment to bear on this question.
As my leader said this afternoon, we in this group regret that in our attempt, as a group of 24 members, to bring our best judgment to bear on the question, we have not all come out with the same conclusion. Regret that fact though we may, I think I can say for my leader as well as for myself that we are proud of the fact that, so far as our party is concerned, we feel that it is our right and our duty to express our personal convictions on this issue and to vote on the motion in the way that each of us feels is best for the future of this country and best for the future of mankind. I hope that members in all other parties will do the same.

Mr. Speaker,
I know of nothing more tormenting or more

North Atlantic Treaty
responsibility. What I did find, however, was that the spokesmen were notorious leaders of communism and communist propaganda. These are the same men who have consistently over the years followed the Moscow line and who are known to be violent, active and unscrupulous agitators for communism. They have previously headed countless delegations to pressure members on a multitude of issues, but all of them pivoting around what would please the Kremlin rather than what is important or basic to the welfare of Canada, its people and the democracies.
The literature they have left convinced me that their concern was more for world communism than for world peace. They made me wary of the classical enjoinder to fear the gifts that the Greeks bring. Their presentation lacked sincerity and was altogether too colourful for me or anyone else to be impressed by their recommendations. It would be folly to be guided by their concern in the matter. Have these selfsame communists who invaded Ottawa ever raised a protest during the past three years, during which time they knew that Russia was arming East Germany to the teeth? Have they condemned the Kremlin by protest meetings, petitions, delegations, and telegrams for the alliance between the Russians and the eastern section of Germany? Are not the Germans in the east the very same type of Germans as in the west? Would it then be healthier, Mr. Speaker, for the preservation of peace to have a strongly armed East Germany and a completely unarmed and defenceless West Germany? This would bring Russian military might to the borders of France. Is that what they would like to see?
What would these selfsame communists do if they were to hear that Western Germany is entering an alliance with Russia and that Russia is arming Germans in the west with every conceivable form of weapon and instrument of destruction? That would certainly please them and I am sure that we would not hear from the infamous peace congress a whimper of protest against Russia for doing exactly what the democracies are now planning to do. To them, what is sauce for the goose is obviously not sauce for the gander.
How stupid and how inconsistent is their position! How effective a case indeed they clearly make out for the approval of the measure before the house! Their vociferous protests and anxiety convince anyone who may be in doubt, and who may be torn between his emotions and his reason, to promptly realize how fatal it would be to follow Moscow's desire in this matter. They help, therefore, provide the answer to the dilemma in which many of us find ourselves.

As I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, to my knowledge there was not, in all the delegations that came to my office, a single person in a position of responsible leadership. I thought it my duty, however, to seek guidance and I carefully canvassed the opinions of the recognized leaders in my own ethnic group across Canada. Nowhere in this responsible leadership was there an opinion other than to uphold the position of our government in its all out effort to halt the advance of communism. But at the same time we should like to caution our government and the democratic leaders of the world that this alliance should not be made without the greatest measure of controls, and safeguards being provided against any possible abuse of the weapons placed in German hands.
In order to achieve this, Mr. Speaker, I should like to call on the government to make certain that, in addition to the safeguards contained in the protocol, there should be further provision that the new German republic should be bound by the genocide pact and the human rights charter under the United Nations Organization. In this way inhuman or discriminatory laws enacted by the republic could be brought before the tribunal of the world, where they could be declared illegal and expunged from the statutes.
We recall, during the Hitler regime, the cries from world Jewish leadership to the democracies that inhuman laws were being enacted and implemented in Germany. The world remained silent. This silence encouraged the horrible legislative process of exterminating millions of innocent people. Under international law, very little else could then have been done. There could be no interference in the domestic affairs of a sovereign state. What a tragic situation that was!
Under the ties presently being established between the NATO countries safeguards must be taken against a possible repetition of such a condition. I should, therefore, like to see either enactments or obligations contractually undertaken that would make it possible to bring before the world tribunal for examination any doubtful law enacted by any member state. The international tribunal could then, if it so found, declare it a contravention of human rights and therefore illegal and inoperative.
With Germany as a member of the family of nations, she would be bound to abide by the decisions of this world tribunal, and could never again enact inhuman or discriminatory laws. She would likewise be obliged to observe and respect the four freedoms, as well as the contractual obligations she will undertake concerning the

limitation of her armanments as set forth in the protocol now before us.
With regard to the sure and careful control of German arms and munitions, as set forth in this protocol, I have every confidence that our military experts have provided adequate safeguards. But more important even than contractual arrangements, in my opinion, will be the assured maintenance of a strong allied land force on the European continent. This will be the best guarantee that the German army is not left free to run havoc with its own resourcefulness. Any complete autonomy given Germany should, therefore, only be agreed to with the proposed limitation of German arms. On that issue I agree completely with the people of France.
In other words, complete autonomy can cover everything with the exception of autonomous control of its army, air force and navy, as well as the extent of its armaments, all of which should remain constantly under the supervision of the western powers in conformity with the terms of the protocol.
Germany should not hesitate to yield to the western powers the fullest long-range guarantees to ensure against a resurgence of her militarism. In fact, Germany should not object to anything that will give the utmost confidence to her allies that she will comply with her obligations. This will also show that she consents to be placed in a position where she will not be able to use her armaments for her own military adventures, either now or in the future, if a changed leadership in Germany should at any time have such notions.
This procedure would also show a measure of atonement for the shameful performance in the past, and would be a genuine earnest of her humility in asking to be admitted to the family of nations once more.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that all my colleagues in the house will bear with me if they find that I have spoken with some emotion on
North Atlantic Treaty
this subject. If I did so,' it is perhaps due to the fact that, to a greater extent than anyone else in the house possibly, I have personally been a victim of nazi cruelty. My rather distressed feelings result not only from the fact that I belong to that ethnic group which suffered most, but also because my own uncles, aunts and cousins, consisting of a family of over 60 persons, were tormented and put to death by the nazis. Hon. members I am sure can therefore appreciate that notwithstanding the over-all record of nazi cruelty and my own personal grief, I am still led to the conclusion to vote in favour of this resolution, I do so only because, to paraphrase a Shakespearean line:
Not that I dislike Berlin less,
But because I fear Moscow more.
By your leave, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make one more personal remark, and it is this: as I stand here before my colleagues on the floor of this house, and as one of the spokesmen of my ethnic group, I most solemnly declare that I vote for the resolution, but not without a deep ache in my heart caused by my grave doubts, apprehensions and misgivings; and I therefore accompany my vote with a most fervent prayer that, in the wisdom of Him who guides the destiny of us all, this vote may be for the betterment of all mankind.
On motion of Miss Aitken the debate was adjourned.
